title: AI Benchmarks: Climbing the Wrong Hills
content:
In 1975, Charles Goodhart, the Chief Adviser to the Bank of England, observed that when governments tried to regulate a set of financial assets, those assets stopped being reliable indicators of economic trends. In what is now known as Goodhart’s Law, he stated that:
“Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.”
Put more simply, when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
For most of AI’s history, AI benchmarks avoided this fate because they measured capabilities that existing models fell meaningfully short of and captured increases driven by a variety of model improvements. As researchers built better methods, higher scores followed not because they deliberately targeted those metrics, but as a side effect of genuine improvement.
This is no longer the case. Recent gains on benchmark performance appear concentrated in areas that frontier labs have explicitly targeted for improvement. Today’s models improve largely through reinforcement learning (RL): a model attempts a task many times, is scored on each attempt, and is pushed toward whatever scored highest, a process called hill climbing. Flawed benchmarks, therefore, not only mismeasure progress against real-world outcomes, but can steer models in the wrong direction.
As AI encompasses a growing share of the global economy, Goodhart’s Law is playing out at a scale it never has before. Big Tech alone plans to spend more than $700 billion on CapEx in 2026, much of it to build and serve models that are ranked, sold, and even bet on according to benchmark scores that often fail to measure what they claim to. That raises the question: are today’s benchmarks still the best way to measure frontier capabilities, or is it time for a new generation? This report covers how and why popular benchmarks are failing, why good ones are so expensive to build, and what better ones could look like.
Benchmarks versus Reality
Few benchmarks show the problem as clearly as Arena (formerly LMArena), a benchmark known for how deliberately labs target it. Launched in May 2023 by UC Berkeley researchers as Chatbot Arena, Arena’s namesake benchmark consists of a platform where users can chat with two anonymous models and vote on which response they prefer in a head-to-head battle. These votes are then converted into a chess-style Elo rating, allowing for direct comparisons of model performance across matchups. By April 2025, the platform drew over one million unique visitors per month and became a mainstay in new-model press releases.
In April 2025, Meta released Llama 4. In the company’s blog post announcing the new model family, it touted that Llama 4 Maverick, a 17 billion active parameter model, beat GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash across a wide range of benchmarks. One such headline number was an experimental chat version of Llama 4 Maverick achieving an Elo of 1417 on Arena, placing it second on the leaderboard and ahead of models released just months prior, including GPT-4.5, Grok 3, and DeepSeek R1.
Source: Mark Zuckerberg
In the days after the model’s release, users found the benchmark scores didn’t reflect reality. A disconnect emerged between the behavior of the model developers could download and the overly verbose, emoji-riddled responses observed in the Maverick version used for head-to-head preference battles on Arena. Users on X quickly pointed out the Maverick version used for the benchmark was “optimized for conversationally,” an assumption found in a chart footnote. At the same time, rumors spread that Meta trained on benchmark test sets, claims the company denied.
In response to growing criticism, Arena retested the unmodified version of Maverick accessible to the general public. It ranked 32nd, below GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro, the last of which was released over a year before Llama 4. At the end of April 2025, Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, admitted that:
“It was relatively easy for our team to tune a version of Llama 4 Maverick that could be way at the top. But the version we released, the pure model, actually has no tuning for that at all, so it’s further down. So you just need to be careful with some of these benchmarks.”
The very same day, researchers released a paper disclosing findings that Meta had privately tested 27 unreleased variants on Arena before launch. The process worked like p-hacking, where researchers can cherry-pick variables, outcomes, or data points to force a statistically significant result (i.e., p-value < 0.05). Just as a scientist who runs enough analyses will eventually find a “significant” result by chance, a lab that tests enough model versions will eventually find one that performs well on the leaderboard.
Source: The Leaderboard Illusion
Arena shared the skepticism directed at Meta. Three days after Maverick’s launch, Gwern, the pseudonymous researcher and writer, flagged major issues with Arena that made it gameable. The people actually rating model responses are all self-selected, and since they are unpaid, they have zero incentive to be honest, rigorous in their judgments, or provide good responses. From this analysis, he posited that:
“It's past time for LMArena people to sit down and have some thorough reflection on whether it is still worth running at all, and at what point they are doing more harm than good.”
The failed launch of Meta’s Maverick model catalyzed a company restructuring, marking the beginning of over a year of reorganization and changes. In May 2025, Meta reportedly delayed the release of its flagship Llama 4 Behemoth, rumored in part because it would not match earlier performance claims. In June 2025, Meta invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI to secure a 49% stake and bring its CEO, Alexandr Wang, into Meta’s leadership to lead the newly formed Meta Superintelligence Labs. That same month, Meta began offering multimillion-dollar pay packages to attract AI research talent. In October 2025, it laid off approximately 600 workers across the AI teams working on pre-Maverick research and products.
In November 2025, Meta’s Chief AI Scientist, Yann LeCun, left the company, later admitting that Llama 4’s “results were fudged a little bit,” with different models being used to achieve better results on different benchmarks. He also underscored the role of Maverick in kickstarting the company-wide changes, stating that:
“Mark was really upset and basically lost confidence in everyone who was involved in this. And so basically sidelined the entire GenAI organization. A lot of people have left, a lot of people who haven’t yet left will leave.”
18 months after Maverick’s launch, the arena that Meta has climbed back to the podium of is little changed from what made it susceptible in the first place. The votes used to calculate model Elo scores still come from anonymous, unpaid Internet users who write their own prompts. Although Arena now filters out duplicate votes and adjusts for style differences by default, it has not changed who gets to cast the votes. The same people who pushed Maverick’s sycophantic behavior to a silver medal are judging today’s model responses. Frontier labs are also still permitted to test an uncapped number of model variants before making them officially public. The results from these unreleased versions are shared privately with the lab, and the lab can withdraw any model version it does not like.
In April 2026, a full year after the release of the Llama 4 model family, Meta introduced Muse Spark. This was followed by the release of Muse Spark 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, and the Muse Wonder models in successive months starting in July 2026. As of October 2026, Meta is once again second on the Arena text leaderboard for all labs, trailing only Anthropic, and Arena has raised $200 million at a $3.1 billion valuation in a Series B funding round.
The same benchmark is even being used to settle Polymarket and Kalshi markets. From February 2025 to October 202

report.summary: A new report argues Goodhart's Law has caught up with AI benchmarks, as labs optimize models for leaderboards like Arena in ways that distort real-world capability signals.
report.background: Since the earliest days of AI research, benchmarks such as ImageNet, GLUE and MMLU measured capabilities models genuinely lacked; rising scores followed real progress rather than targeted optimization. Modern training changed that dynamic. Frontier models are largely refined through reinforcement learning, where a model attempts tasks repeatedly, gets scored, and is pushed toward whatever earns the highest reward — a hill-climbing process that turns any flawed metric into an explicit objective. With Big Tech alone planning over $700 billion in capital expenditure for 2026, and benchmark scores used to rank, sell, and even settle prediction markets on models, the stakes of mismeasurement are higher than ever. The report traces how this dynamic played out publicly with Meta's Llama 4 Maverick, and asks whether today's benchmarks can still serve as reliable proxies for frontier capability.
key_points: Goodhart's Law has arrived in AI: when a benchmark score becomes a target that labs optimize for, it stops being a trustworthy measure of capability. Historical benchmarks avoided this because models fell far short of them and progress came from many independent improvements; today's RL-driven training lets labs climb specific leaderboard hills directly.

Arena (formerly Chatbot Arena) is the clearest example. Meta's Llama 4 Maverick hit an Elo of 1417 using an experimentally 'conversationally optimized' variant, but the public model ranked 32nd when retested — below GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro, released over a year earlier.

Benchmarks are gameable by design. Researchers found Meta privately tested 27 unreleased model variants on Arena before launch, akin to p-hacking: test enough versions and one will land high on the leaderboard. Arena's voters are self-selected, unpaid internet users with little incentive for rigor, and labs can withdraw results they dislike.

The fallout was severe and lasting. Zuckerberg conceded the tuned model was easy to top the charts with, LeCun later said Llama 4's 'results were fudged a little bit,' and Meta reorganized its AI teams — a $14.3 billion Scale AI stake, new superintelligence lab, and roughly 600 AI layoffs in October 2025.

Arena has changed little. It now filters duplicate votes and adjusts for style, but the same anonymous voters judge responses and labs still test an uncapped number of private variants. Meanwhile Arena raised $200 million at a $3.1 billion valuation and its Elo scores even settle Polymarket and Kalshi markets.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report signals that leaderboard leadership is an increasingly weak signal of real capability, undermining how enterprises choose vendors and how investors value labs. For developers, it means benchmark-topping models may underperform in production — the Llama 4 gap between the tuned and shipped versions is the cautionary tale — so private, task-specific evaluations matter more than public Elo. For regular users, the risk is subtler: models trained to win preference votes learn sycophancy, verbosity, and emoji-heavy styling rather than accuracy or usefulness, since humans reward flattering answers. If benchmarks also shape prediction markets and procurement, distorted metrics propagate into real economic decisions. The likely correction is a shift toward expensive, private, contamination-resistant evals that labs cannot repeatedly hill-climb against.
report.tools: To evaluate models more skeptically, watch LiveBench (contamination-resistant, regularly refreshed tasks), SWE-bench and its variants for coding agents, HELM from Stanford for holistic evaluation, and Artificial Analysis for independent multi-benchmark comparisons. Epoch AI tracks capability trends beyond leaderboards. The 'Leaderboard Illusion' paper (arXiv, 2025) documents Arena gaming directly and is worth reading alongside this report. Teams deploying models should build small internal eval suites from real production tasks rather than trusting public Elo rankings.
